cards.front: Recall a key point about Additive Manufacturing
cards.back: Additive manufacturing builds components layer by layer from a digital model, adding material rather than removing it.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Additive Manufacturing
cards.back: Fused Deposition Modelling (FDM) extrudes thermoplastic filament through a heated nozzle; the most common and affordable 3D printing method.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Additive Manufacturing
cards.back: Selective Laser Sintering (SLS) uses a laser to fuse powdered material (nylon, metal) layer by layer; produces strong, functional parts.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Additive Manufacturing
cards.back: Stereolithography (SLA) uses a UV laser to cure liquid resin; produces very high-resolution parts with smooth surface finish.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Additive Manufacturing
cards.back: Key advantages: complex geometries, no tooling required, minimal waste, rapid iteration, customisation and on-demand production.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Additive Manufacturing
cards.back: Limitations: slower than mass-production methods, limited material range, anisotropic properties (weaker between layers), surface finish may need post-processing.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Additive Manufacturing
cards.back: Support structures are needed for overhangs in FDM and SLA; these must be removed after printing.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Additive Manufacturing
cards.back: Metal additive manufacturing uses powdered metal (stainless steel, titanium, aluminium) and laser or electron beam sintering.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Additive Manufacturing
cards.back: Rapid prototyping allows engineers to test form, fit and function before committing to expensive production tooling.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Additive Manufacturing
cards.back: CAD files are converted to STL format then sliced into layers by the printer software.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Additive Manufacturing
cards.back: Additive manufacturing reduces waste compared to subtractive processes because material is only deposited where needed.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Additive Manufacturing
cards.back: Aerospace, medical and automotive industries are the main users of high-end additive manufacturing.

cards.front: What should you know about gcse engineering exam tips — additive manufacturing?
cards.back: 1. For Additive Manufacturing questions, use precise design and technology terminology 2. Consider function, aesthetics, ergonomics, sustainability and cost in your answers 3. When evaluating, justify your design decisions with reference to user needs and specifications 4. Show your understanding of Additive Manufacturing through both theory and practical application 5. Reference real products and manufacturing processes where relevant
